papers.title: Zero-Shot Protein–Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
papers.summary: Abstract Motivation Accurate identification of protein–ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Results Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands. Availability and Implementation The source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/mahdip72/ProteinLigand . The datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23042604

papers.llm_rss_summary_zh: 准确识别蛋白质-配体结合位点对于机械生物学和药物发现至关重要，但不同配体家族和数据可用性体系的预测性能差异很大。我们提出了一个系统的配体感知基准和评估框架，用于跨三种设置的残基水平结合位点预测：具有丰富示例的过度代表性配体、具有有限示例的代表性不足的配体以及训练期间未见的零样本配体。结果使用具有配体特异性序列聚类的 BioLiP2 衍生数据集，我们评估了旨在研究这些机制的渐进式三阶段基于序列的建模套件。第 1 阶段使用预训练的蛋白质语言模型 (PLM) 训练配体特异性预测因子。第二阶段通过学习嵌入引入配体调节，从而实现单一多配体模型。第 3 阶段将这些嵌入替换为在 SMILES 上运行的预训练化学语言模型 (CLM) 的表示形式，从而能够预测以前未见过的配体。在最初的三阶段比较中，尽管比较同时改变了预测器架构、配体调节和训练方案，但阶段 2 在代表性测试集上实现了比阶段 1 更高的配体宏 F1（0.5832 与 0.4769）。第 2 阶段的性能也优于多个基于序列和结构的基线。第 3 阶段在以前未见过的配体上实现了 0.3109 的合并残基水平 F1 和 0.2338 的配体宏 F1，同时在代表配体上保持竞争性。 使用恒定、不匹配和混乱的 SMILES 输入的对照实验降低了所有三种测试方案的性能，这提供了模型使用与所提供的配体输入相关的信息而不是仅仅依赖于通用蛋白质结合位点倾向的证据。五个 PLM 规模和多个 CLM 的消融进一步表明，增加 PLM 规模通常会提高性能，尽管趋势并不严格单调，而 CLM 规模扩大会产生较小且不太一致的增益。总的来说，这项研究提供了一个系统基准，用于量化配体数据可用性对残基水平结合位点预测的影响，并评估对以前未见过的配体的泛化。可用性和实施​​源代码和模型权重可在 https://github.com/mahdip72/ProteinLigand 获取。数据集可在 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23042604 获取

papers.primary_summary_raw:
MOTIVATION: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training.

RESULTS: Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/mahdip72/ProteinLigand. The datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23042604.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: MetaHQ: Harmonized, high-quality metadata annotations of public omics samples and studies
papers.summary: Abstract Summary Public omics databases like the Gene Expression Omnibus and the Sequence Read Archive offer substantial opportunities for data reuse to address novel biomedical questions. However, it is still difficult to find samples and studies of interest since they are described by free-text metadata and lack standardized annotations. To address this issue, multiple research groups have undertaken curation efforts to add standardized annotations to large collections of these data, but these annotations are fragmented across online resources and are stored in different formats subject to varying standardization criteria, hindering the integration of annotations across sources. We developed MetaHQ to harmonize and distribute standardized metadata for public omics samples. MetaHQ comprises a database with annotations for >567k samples and >27k studies in GEO from 13 sources and a user-friendly command-line interface (CLI) to query the database and retrieve annotations. Availability and implementation The MetaHQ CLI is deployed as a Python Package on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/metahq-cli that accesses the MetaHQ database available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17663086 . Project source code and documentation are available at https://github.com/krishnanlab/meta-hq

papers.title: Meta2Data: Automated data processing for large scale microbiome data re-analysis
papers.summary: Summary Meta2Data is a modular, largely automated pipeline implemented in Python and Bash for the retrieval, standardization, and processing of public microbiome sequencing data. It retrieves metadata from major public repositories, including INSDC and CNCB, using user-provided keywords or BioProject/BioSample identifiers. Retrieved metadata are standardized using a synonym dictionary and then subjected to manual curation. Based on the curated metadata, Meta2Data downloads the corresponding raw sequencing data and processes them using standardized workflows based on DADA2 or VSEARCH. The pipeline supports both single- and multiple-target-region datasets and produces integrated feature tables, taxonomic assignments, and phylogenetic trees for downstream microbial community analyses. Availability Meta2Data is freely available at https://github.com/LinyangSun/Meta2Data and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20670433

papers.title: Deep learning-based enhancing spatial biological context parsing
papers.summary: Abstract Motivation The rapid advancement of spatial transcriptomics (ST) has established a foundation for the complementary integration of multimodal information from gene expression profiles, spatial localization, and histological images. However, noise and data heterogeneity complicate the characterization of spatial relationships and tissue structure. Results In this study, we develop a deep learning framework, CroSP, based on a multi-view graph autoencoder. The framework integrates gene expression profiles, spatial locations, and tissue morphology information into a low-dimensional latent representation. Cross-view contrastive learning and metric learning coordinate the complementary views. Across datasets from multiple platforms and spatial resolutions, CroSP improved spatial domain identification and delineated brain and olfactory bulb structures. Analyses using established downstream methods further characterized spatially variable genes and the spatial heterogeneity, immune microenvironments, and cell–cell communication in human breast cancer tissue. These results support the use of CroSP for spatial biological analysis in healthy and diseased tissues. Availability and Implementation Source code and tutorials: https://github.com/Biowust/CroSP.git . Archived code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22675113 . Public raw datasets: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22533825

papers.primary_summary_raw: The rapid advancement of spatial transcriptomics (ST) has established a foundation for the complementary integration of multimodal information from gene expression profiles, spatial localization, and histological images. However, noise and data heterogeneity complicate the characterization of spatial relationships and tissue structure. Results In this study, we develop a deep learning framework, CroSP, based on a multi-view graph autoencoder. The framework integrates gene expression profiles, spatial locations, and tissue morphology information into a low-dimensional latent representation. Cross-view contrastive learning and metric learning coordinate the complementary views. Across datasets from multiple platforms and spatial resolutions, CroSP improved spatial domain identification and delineated brain and olfactory bulb structures. Analyses using established downstream methods further characterized spatially variable genes and the spatial heterogeneity, immune microenvironments, and cell–cell communication in human breast cancer tissue. These results support the use of CroSP for spatial biological analysis in healthy and diseased tissues.

papers.title: CryoET-DDM: restoring high-fidelity signals in cryo-electron tomography via a data-driven diffusion model
papers.summary: Abstract Motivation Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is an essential technique for resolving high-resolution structures of macromolecular complexes in situ . However, the extremely low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in tilt series, caused by strict electron dose limitations, remains a major bottleneck for subtomogram averaging (STA). Although existing denoising methods can enhance tomogram contrast, they may compromise the high-frequency structural information required for downstream STA refinement. Results We introduce CryoET-DDM, a diffusion framework for high-fidelity restoration of cryo-ET tilt series that integrates data-driven noise modeling and fidelity-guided structural preservation. CryoET-DDM incorporates background noise patches extracted from the same experimental tilt series into the diffusion process to model the noise characteristics of low-dose imaging. A fidelity-guided learning objective promotes structural consistency during denoising, helping preserve high-frequency information needed for STA. Experiments on three public datasets (EMPIAR-10499, EMPIAR-10164, and EMPIAR-10651) show that CryoET-DDM improves particle quality, preserves structural fidelity, and yields downstream gains in STA resolution. These results support tilt series denoising as a promising strategy for cryo-ET data processing and improve the reliability of in situ structural biology analysis. Availability and implementation Code and models for our experiments are available at https://github.com/xinsheng44/CryoET-DDM . The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR

all_papers.title: Zero-Shot Protein–Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
all_papers.summary: Abstract Motivation Accurate identification of protein–ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Results Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands. Availability and Implementation The source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/mahdip72/ProteinLigand . The datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23042604

all_papers.primary_summary_raw:
MOTIVATION: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training.

RESULTS: Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The source code and model weights are available at https://github.com/mahdip72/ProteinLigand. The datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23042604.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

all_papers.title: CryoET-DDM: restoring high-fidelity signals in cryo-electron tomography via a data-driven diffusion model
all_papers.summary: Abstract Motivation Cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) is an essential technique for resolving high-resolution structures of macromolecular complexes in situ . However, the extremely low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in tilt series, caused by strict electron dose limitations, remains a major bottleneck for subtomogram averaging (STA). Although existing denoising methods can enhance tomogram contrast, they may compromise the high-frequency structural information required for downstream STA refinement. Results We introduce CryoET-DDM, a diffusion framework for high-fidelity restoration of cryo-ET tilt series that integrates data-driven noise modeling and fidelity-guided structural preservation. CryoET-DDM incorporates background noise patches extracted from the same experimental tilt series into the diffusion process to model the noise characteristics of low-dose imaging. A fidelity-guided learning objective promotes structural consistency during denoising, helping preserve high-frequency information needed for STA. Experiments on three public datasets (EMPIAR-10499, EMPIAR-10164, and EMPIAR-10651) show that CryoET-DDM improves particle quality, preserves structural fidelity, and yields downstream gains in STA resolution. These results support tilt series denoising as a promising strategy for cryo-ET data processing and improve the reliability of in situ structural biology analysis. Availability and implementation Code and models for our experiments are available at https://github.com/xinsheng44/CryoET-DDM . The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR

all_papers.summary: Abstract Motivation The rapid advancement of spatial transcriptomics (ST) has established a foundation for the complementary integration of multimodal information from gene expression profiles, spatial localization, and histological images. However, noise and data heterogeneity complicate the characterization of spatial relationships and tissue structure. Results In this study, we develop a deep learning framework, CroSP, based on a multi-view graph autoencoder. The framework integrates gene expression profiles, spatial locations, and tissue morphology information into a low-dimensional latent representation. Cross-view contrastive learning and metric learning coordinate the complementary views. Across datasets from multiple platforms and spatial resolutions, CroSP improved spatial domain identification and delineated brain and olfactory bulb structures. Analyses using established downstream methods further characterized spatially variable genes and the spatial heterogeneity, immune microenvironments, and cell–cell communication in human breast cancer tissue. These results support the use of CroSP for spatial biological analysis in healthy and diseased tissues. However, it is still difficult to find samples and studies of interest since they are described by free-text metadata and lack standardized annotations. To address this issue, multiple research groups have undertaken curation efforts to add standardized annotations to large collections of these data, but these annotations are fragmented across online resources and are stored in different formats subject to varying standardization criteria, hindering the integration of annotations across sources. We developed MetaHQ to harmonize and distribute standardized metadata for public omics samples. MetaHQ comprises a database with annotations for >567k samples and >27k studies in GEO from 13 sources and a user-friendly command-line interface (CLI) to query the database and retrieve annotations. Availability and implementation The MetaHQ CLI is deployed as a Python Package on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/metahq-cli that accesses the MetaHQ database available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17663086 . Project source code and documentation are available at https://github.com/krishnanlab/meta-hq

all_papers.title: Meta2Data: Automated data processing for large scale microbiome data re-analysis
all_papers.summary: Summary Meta2Data is a modular, largely automated pipeline implemented in Python and Bash for the retrieval, standardization, and processing of public microbiome sequencing data. It retrieves metadata from major public repositories, including INSDC and CNCB, using user-provided keywords or BioProject/BioSample identifiers. Retrieved metadata are standardized using a synonym dictionary and then subjected to manual curation. Based on the curated metadata, Meta2Data downloads the corresponding raw sequencing data and processes them using standardized workflows based on DADA2 or VSEARCH. The pipeline supports both single- and multiple-target-region datasets and produces integrated feature tables, taxonomic assignments, and phylogenetic trees for downstream microbial community analyses. Availability Meta2Data is freely available at https://github.com/LinyangSun/Meta2Data and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20670433
